definition: A measure put in place to reduce risk to systems, data, people or buildings.
How a control is implemented: technical, managerial, operational or physical.
What a control does about an incident: preventive, deterrent, detective, corrective, compensating or directive.
A control implemented by hardware, software or firmware, such as a firewall rule, encryption or antivirus.
A control based on management's oversight of risk, such as a risk assessment, a security policy or a supplier review.
A control carried out by people as part of day-to-day work, such as security awareness training.
A tangible barrier or device that protects buildings and equipment, such as a lock, fence or bollard.
A control that stops an unwanted action from succeeding, such as a firewall rule or a door lock.
A control that discourages an attempt, for example by warning of consequences or of being caught, without blocking it.
A control that identifies and reports an incident during or after it, without stopping it, such as an IDS alert or a log review.
A control that repairs damage and restores normal operation after an incident, such as restoring files from backup.
An approved alternative used when a required control cannot be implemented. It reduces the same risk to a similar level.
A control that tells people what they must or must not do, such as a policy, procedure or instruction sign.
An intrusion detection system only alerts, so it is detective. An intrusion prevention system blocks the traffic, so it is preventive.
The three goals of security: confidentiality, integrity and availability.
Only authorized people and systems can read the information. Protected by encryption and access permissions.
Information is accurate and is changed only by those allowed to change it. Checked with hashes and digital signatures.
Systems and data can be reached when authorized users need them. Protected by redundancy, backups and patching.
A person cannot credibly deny an action, because proof exists that only they could have produced, such as a digital signature.
Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting: prove who you are, receive only the access you are allowed, and have your activity recorded.
Claiming an identity, for example by typing a username. The claim proves nothing until it is authenticated.
Proving a claimed identity, for example with a password, a token, a fingerprint or a certificate.
Deciding what an authenticated user or device is allowed to access or do.
Recording what users and devices do: sign-in time, resources used, data transferred and sign-out time.
Proving a person's identity with factors: something you know, something you have, something you are (objective 4.6 adds somewhere you are). Two different factors make multifactor authentication.
Proving the identity of a device or service, usually with a digital certificate issued by a certificate authority the organization trusts.
A consistent method for deciding access, by roles, attributes, rules or labels, so that permissions are not set by hand for each user.
A comparison of current security with a target standard or baseline. It produces a list of shortfalls and a plan to close them.
A model in which no user or device is trusted because of its network location. Every access request is authenticated and authorized.
The part of a Zero Trust architecture that makes and communicates access decisions. It contains the policy engine and the policy administrator.
The part of a Zero Trust architecture that carries the actual traffic between subject and resource, through the policy enforcement point.
Zero Trust control-plane concept: adjusting how much proof of identity is required by using context such as location, device, time and behavior.
Zero Trust control-plane concept: limiting an attacker's entry points and how far a compromise can spread, through least privilege, segmentation and small implicit trust zones.
Zero Trust control-plane concept: deciding each access request from defined policies that combine identity, device and context, not from network location.
Zero Trust control-plane component that decides whether to grant, deny or revoke access for each request.
Zero Trust control-plane component that carries out the policy engine's decision by telling the policy enforcement point to open or close a session.
Zero Trust data-plane gatekeeper in the traffic path. It allows, monitors and ends connections as the policy administrator instructs.
The area behind a policy enforcement point where traffic is not checked again. Zero Trust keeps it as small as possible.
In Zero Trust, the user, application or service requesting access (subject) and the device it uses (system). Both are verified.
Short, sturdy posts that stop vehicles from reaching a building while letting pedestrians walk through.
A small room with two interlocking doors that admits one verified person at a time. It prevents tailgating. Formerly called a mantrap.
A barrier that encloses the site perimeter. It deters intruders and slows them down.
Cameras that are watched live or recorded (CCTV). They detect activity, provide evidence afterwards and deter when visible.
A person who checks identification, handles visitors and responds to incidents. Adds human judgment that the other physical controls in this objective lack.
An ID card read by door readers. It identifies the holder, and each use is logged with the door and the time.
A physical control that removes dark areas where intruders could approach unseen, and lets guards and cameras see.
Detects infrared radiation (heat), such as a warm body moving across its view. Works in light and in darkness.
Detects a change in weight or force on a surface, such as a step on a floor mat or an object being lifted.
Detects movement by sending out microwave (radio) pulses and measuring the reflections. Covers large areas; the signal passes through thin walls.
Detects movement by sending out sound waves above human hearing and measuring the reflections. The sound stays inside the room.
Decoys with no business use, planted to detect attackers, waste their time and reveal their methods. Any interaction with a decoy is suspicious.
A single decoy system made to look like a real, attractive target, used to detect and observe attackers.
A network of honeypots that imitates a real environment, showing how attackers move between systems.
A bait file with a tempting name placed on a real system. Opening it raises an alert.
A piece of fake, tracked data, such as a record or login details. If it is used or appears elsewhere, data has been stolen.
The formal process for controlling changes to systems: each change is requested, assessed, tested, approved, scheduled, implemented, verified and documented.
The formal review in which approvers, often a change advisory board, weigh the impact analysis and test results and decide whether a change may proceed.
A group from IT, security and the business that reviews change requests and approves, rejects or returns them. Also called a change control board.
Accountability for a change from request to sign-off. The owner usually owns the affected system or data, and need not perform the change. The approval body decides.
Everyone a change affects. They are consulted about its impact and told what will happen and when.
An assessment made before a change of which systems and users it affects, what could go wrong, and the risk of not making it.
Recorded evidence from trying a change in a test environment, showing whether it works and leaves security settings intact. Approvers expect it before deciding.
The documented way to return a system to its previous working state if a change fails: a restore point, written steps and a decision point.
An agreed period, chosen to disturb the business least, during which an approved change may be made.
Written step-by-step instructions for a routine task, so that it is done the same way every time.
A list of permitted items, such as applications or addresses. Anything not on the list is blocked.
A list of blocked items, such as applications or addresses. Anything not on the list is permitted.
The limit an approval places on a change: only the approved actions, on the approved systems, in the approved window. Anything else must go back through the change process.
A period when a service is unavailable to its users. Changes should plan it, keep it short and place it in the maintenance window.
Stopping and starting one background service so that it loads a change, while the operating system and other services keep running.
Closing and reopening a program so that it loads a new version or settings. Its users may lose sessions or unsaved work.
An old application the business still relies on that is no longer supported or well understood, so changes around it are risky.
Cases where one component needs another to work, so changing one can break others or force them to change first.
Revising network and data flow diagrams after a change so that they still match the real environment.
Revising written policies and procedures when a change alters how work is done, so that people do not follow outdated instructions.
Tracking every version of a file, such as code or a configuration: who changed what, when and why, with the ability to restore earlier versions.
An urgent change that takes a faster approval route and is documented right afterward. It is still approved and recorded.
